abstract: Lichtinger and Hosseini critically examine the influential narrative that AI is an 'inequality equalizer' based on prominent experimental studies. While acknowledging that multiple well-identified experiments consistently show AI narrows within-task performance gaps — with lower-performing workers benefiting disproportionately from AI assistance — they argue these findings cannot be extrapolated to broader inequality conclusions. The authors identify three critical channels omitted by experimental designs: (1) task uniformity, since experiments hold tasks constant while real-world workers at different seniority levels perform fundamentally different work, with junior staff doing more routine, codifiable tasks that are more exposed to AI displacement; (2) the augmentation-versus-automation distinction, where studies capture only tool-assisted productivity gains but miss firm decisions to eliminate tasks entirely, which the authors consider the channel with the largest potential inequality effects; and (3) labor supply dynamics, where AI reduces entry barriers to high-skill occupations, intensifying competitive pressure. Drawing on their own empirical research (Hosseini and Lichtinger 2025, 2026), they present evidence that junior employment declines sharply at AI-adopting firms relative to non-adopters while senior employment remains unaffected, and that predicted productivity gains appear larger for high-expertise occupations — patterns that directly contradict the within-task equalization narrative. They conclude that whether AI reduces or exacerbates inequality remains a genuinely open question.
keyFindings: Prominent experiments consistently show AI narrows within-task performance gaps: Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) found a 30% increase in issues resolved per hour for less experienced customer-support agents; Noy and Zhang (2023) found 0.45 standard deviation quality improvement with larger gains for lower-scoring workers; Dell'Acqua et al. (2023) found 43% quality improvement for lower-performing consultants versus 17% for top-half performers.

These experimental findings cannot be generalized to economy-wide inequality because experiments hold tasks constant, but junior and senior workers perform fundamentally different tasks in practice — with junior work being more routine, codifiable, and exposed to AI displacement.

Hosseini and Lichtinger (2025) find that after generative AI adoption, junior employment declines sharply relative to non-adopters while senior employment is largely unaffected, contradicting the equalization narrative.

The automation channel — firms deciding not to assign tasks to workers at all — is identified as having the largest potential effects on inequality but is entirely missed by augmentation-focused experiments.

Cruces et al. (2026) found AI closes about 75% of the baseline productivity gap between education groups in experimental settings, but this within-task finding may not translate to between-occupation outcomes.
methodology: Analytical review synthesizing findings from multiple randomized controlled experiments (Brynjolfsson et al. 2025; Noy and Zhang 2023; Dell'Acqua et al. 2023; Cruces et al. 2026) alongside the authors' own empirical research using firm-level adoption data (Hosseini and Lichtinger 2025, 2026). The critique applies a structural economic framework distinguishing within-task augmentation effects from between-occupation automation and labor supply dynamics to evaluate the external validity of experimental results.
qualifiers: The authors do not claim AI definitively increases inequality — they argue the question remains genuinely open. Their critique is primarily structural rather than empirically comprehensive; the firm-level evidence on junior versus senior employment effects may reflect early adoption patterns that could shift over time. The analysis focuses on knowledge work and does not address AI's effects on manual or service occupations. Between-occupation inequality effects depend on future deployment patterns that are inherently uncertain.
